newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA CABINET APPROVES 1997 BUDGET FRAME.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA CABINET APPROVES 1997 BUDGET FRAME.

text.p: Bulgaria's government on Friday
completed approval of the 1997 consolidated state budget draft
as part of preparations to launch a currency board system on
July 1, Finance Minister Muravei Radev said.
"The cabinet approved this year's budget and will submit it
to (committees in) parliament on Monday for approval by the end
of the month," Radev told reporters.
A deficit of 5.81 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
was assumed in the central government budget and a deficit of
6.16 percent was projected in the broader consolidated state
budget, which also includes the budgets of the judicial system,
the ministries and the municipalities.
GDP was assumed at 16,150 billion levs, down a real 7.4
percent from 1996, calculated through a deflator of 950.5
percent, said Radev. GDP fell a real 10.9 percent last year to
1,660.2 billion levs.
Figures in billion levs follow unless stated otherwise:
CENTRAL GVT BUDGET CONSOLIDATED BUDGET
REVENUE 2,688 4,703
pct of GDP 16.64 29.12
SPENDING 3,625 5,698
pct of GDP 22.45 35.28
DEFICIT -937 -995
pct of GDP 5.81 6.16
The consolidated budget deficit of 6.16 percent was higher
than IMF-recommended 3.8 percent due to pending interest
payments on Bulgarian foreign and domestic debt, but lower than
last year's 13 percent.
An exchange rate of 1,000 levs per mark was assumed in the
budget as Bulgaria is to introduce on July 1 an IMF-prescribed
restrictive fixed exchange rate mechanism, called a currency
board, to stabilise the economy.
Annual inflation was seen at 566 percent at end-1997 with
average monthly inflation rate expected at 1.5-2.0 percent in
the second half and around one percent by year's end.
Monthly consumer price inflation for May was 5.6 percent,
bringing cumulative inflation for the first five months to
479.4 percent. Annual inflation for last year was 310.8
percent.
Radev said that a trade surplus of over 200 billion levs
was assumed in the budget bill as exports were expected to rise
in the second half of 1997.
A current account surplus was also assumed in the budget
draft and a capital account surplus of $590 million was
expected, said Radev.
He added that a totally non-inflationary deficit financing
was provided for in the draft through proceeds from
privatisation, improved tax collection, domestic debt
restructuring and foreign funding.
Central bank lending to the government and commercial banks
will be banned under the currency board system and levs in
circulation must be fully covered by foreign exchange reserves
at a fixed rate of 1,000 levs per mark.
State subsidies will be reduced but will remain in force
this year for socially-sensitive sectors like railway and city
transport and central heating, Radev said.
Social security payments were assumed at 1.577 trillion
levs, defence was alloted 390 billion levs, interior ministry
222 billion levs and state health service 469 billion levs.
Salary payments in the state sector were assumed at 600
billion levs of which some 200 billion levs were distributed in
the first half of 1997.
